# A1. How pension designs shape the equilibria {#arg-designs}

Each point of the figure is an economy that has always had one pension design, the universal pension ε on the
horizontal axis and the design θ, the weight on earnings-related benefits, in the color, read in 2010 under log preferences; every other parameter
is the paper's calibration. A higher universal pension raises the equilibrium tax rate and lowers the savings rate, the
workweek and the savings of informal relative to formal households. A more Bismarckian design lowers the tax rate
and raises the savings rate and the workweek. The black line is the calibrated θ, and its two markers are the
pre-reform ε and the universal level the reform installs. Between them the tax rate rises by more than the reform
raises it on impact in section {{< var p.sec_argentina >}}: here informal households have always saved under the
universal system, while on impact the retirees of 2010 hold savings made under the old one. The rise between the
markers is close to the reform's effect in 2040, once those savings have adjusted.
